item.description: Uber burning through its 2026 token budget in 13 weeks proves stuffing context is wrong; MongoDB points Agent performance bottlenecks to memory—write, change, recall, forget—and suggests starting with employee use cases and human-in-the-loop.
item.content:encoded:
Uber burning through its 2026 token budget in 13 weeks proves stuffing context is wrong; MongoDB points Agent performance bottlenecks to memory—write, change, recall, forget—and suggests starting with employee use cases and human-in-the-loop.

This episode clears obstacles for Agent engineers: how to set chunk size, the 100k vector threshold, who writes and deletes memory; less valuable for those only interested in model progress.

6:32 Database schemas follow the scarcest resource
Pete anchors on E.F. Codd's 1970 relational model paper: when storage was priciest, normalized tables were rational. By 2007, when MongoDB emerged, the scarce resource had become time, so the document model deliberately denormalizes, using JSON/BSON to cut disk reads. He also corrects a misread positioning: MongoDB is not 'schemaless' but 'schema-flexible'—the same collection can hold documents of different shapes, letting the schema evolve with the product. This design logic shows: database schemas should follow whatever resource is scarcest at the time.

16:38 Stuffing context with data degrades quality
Uber burning through its 2026 token budget in 13 weeks is treated as a failed token-maxing strategy. Cost is only half the problem; quality drops too: studies show the first and last few thousand tokens matter most, the middle is mostly noise. This pushes the industry toward 'classified memory'—selecting only a few relevant terms per agent loop rather than replaying all history. The key isn't saving money but that attention decay inside the context makes selective retrieval a performance issue.

23:21 AI features grow from where customers already hurt
MongoDB's search capabilities grew layer by layer from customer pain points: lexical search in 2020 because many were building Lucene themselves; then vector search because vectors are essentially float arrays that naturally fit as a document field; then combining lexical, vector, and metadata pre-filtering into one hybrid search. In 2025 they acquired Voyage AI to bring embedding models in-house, forming a 'better together' offering. This sequence itself shows: infrastructure companies touching AI features usually start from where customers already hurt, not by buying models first and inventing use cases.

40:10 Chunk size tuning should be delegated to the model
The first nagging RAG problem is chunk size: too small, context insufficient, retrieval quality poor; too large, storage grows and precision drops, requiring manual trial and error. Voyage's 'contextual chunking' sends the sentence and extra context as two strings into the model, which automatically decides the optimal chunk size and returns a single vector. This achieves near-full-context retrieval quality with small chunks and lower storage cost, now in its fourth version. It's a concrete example of moving an engineer's iterative tuning into model weights.

48:20 Embedding models aren't commoditized; selection drives hallucinations
Pete gives two selection thresholds: on scale, you really start to feel pain around 100k vectors; on quality, Voyage leads Hugging Face's RTEB benchmark, improving retrieval by up to 14% over other embedding models—a gap that can directly manifest as hallucinations. He also warns embedding models aren't commoditized—Anthropic doesn't make its own embedding model, so his advice is to use Voyage directly. For many teams, embedding model selection has long been underrated; this segment puts it back at the center of performance and hallucinations.

1:01:05 Memory has a half-life and must be actively retired
Why is memory hard? Pete's analogy: the industry has built databases for sixty years, but agents for about eighteen months. Long-term context strategy is no longer stuffing the whole conversation back; it's recalling best context at query time and writing new facts back to memory after answering; enterprise systems use RBAC to control memory sharing and isolation. He sums up the loop with a colleague's phrase: Write, change, recall, forget. Memory has a half-life—recent info matters more than weeks or months old. This means agent memory must be a first-class citizen, with intentional writes, updates, and eviction.

1:13:10 First enterprise AI wave lands on employees, not customers
Most Fortune 500 companies Pete talks to are doing employee-facing use cases with humans in the loop. Two reasons: ROI is easier to calculate—these roles already have KPIs—and data security consequences are lighter; employee data leaks are easier to handle than customer data. Conversely, fully autonomous customer-facing agents are a worse risk-reward bet right now. This provides a coordinate for enterprise AI budget judgments: the first wave is more likely in internal efficiency tools than in robots making final decisions for customers.

1:24:24 Most sophisticated customers aren't in the US but in Mexico City and São Paulo
Pete met this year's most sophisticated customers in Mexico City and São Paulo, and these customers typically assume US competitors are more advanced. He says he sees the opposite. He attributes this to the ubiquity of hyperscale data centers and AI services—geography matters less than in the cloud era, leveling global access to technology. This observation suggests country labels are increasingly unreliable for judging whether a company can use cutting-edge AI.

item.title: Fed Chairs Never Lose a Vote: Warsh Talks Against Forward Guidance, but His Path Is Paved for Hikes
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-oddlots-warsh演讲只是b-嘴上反指引-身体要加息/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-oddlots-warsh演讲只是b-嘴上反指引-身体要加息/
item.description: Posen gives Warsh's Jackson Hole speech a B-, saying he talks against forward guidance but is actually paving the way for rate hikes, and predicts the Fed will hike 75-100 basis points over the next six months.
item.content:encoded:
Posen gives Warsh's Jackson Hole speech a B-, saying he talks against forward guidance but is actually paving the way for rate hikes, and predicts the Fed will hike 75-100 basis points over the next six months.

Posen is one of the few central bank watchers who dares to talk about 'fiscal dominance.' This episode has hard judgments on Fed governance risks, Powell's legacy, and AI's employment impact—high information density.

4:07 Warsh didn't say hike, but the whole speech was paving the way
Posen gives Warsh's Jackson Hole speech a B-, but considering the chaos of the previous two months, it can be treated as a B+. The fourth section systematically lists reasons inflation could persist or even rise, yet never says 'therefore we must tighten.' Posen sees this as deliberate groundwork: if no hike follows, markets will speculate it's a capitulation to Trump's pressure. He himself has been advocating hikes for months because inflation is real. Warsh also reaffirmed the 2% core PCE target and refused to use wage inflation as a forecasting indicator—all mainstream moves.

8:14 Without defining the 'right pace,' returning to target is empty talk
Posen's biggest concern is that Warsh concluded his speech by saying inflation needs to fall in the 'right direction' at the 'right pace,' without ever defining what the right pace is. Without a pace constraint, 'return to target' is empty talk. From the confirmation hearing, two press conferences, to the ECB Sintra speech, Warsh has reserved the right to decide 'at the last minute,' refusing to pre-commit to his own indicators. This is close to Greenspan's 1999 style, but Greenspan could sustain it through personal ability and control of the committee; once a mistake is made, the whole credibility collapses.

12:20 A Fed chair never loses a single vote
Posen explains the Fed's committee culture: unlike the ECB, which seeks consensus, the Fed has historically given the chair more power. More critically, there's an unwritten rule—only a few dissent per meeting, and the chair never loses a vote. When Volcker found he might lose, he simply announced it would be his last meeting. This culture makes the committee's ability to correct the chair very weak, so Warsh's 'reserved discretion' style carries more risk than he imagines.

19:26 Bashing the central bank isn't dangerous; making it sell government debt is
Posen distinguishes two types of political pressure: ordinary bashing of the central bank is part of the game and can even help the central bank 'take the blame' when necessary. What's truly dangerous is when a president or treasury secretary asks the central bank to help sell government debt—the central bank must answer: 'I'm here to help you and your successor sell debt,' and must never engage in manipulation or cheating. Trump's threats to the Fed are far more serious than rhetoric—trying to strip regional Fed presidents of voting rights, disrupt staggered terms, change the mandate, and touch the budget directly undermine functional independence.

24:34 The most radical reform might be making the central bank talk less
Posen thinks the communications committee led by Mervyn King is most likely to produce radical proposals. King himself is a founder of inflation targeting and fan charts, but after retirement he has publicly doubted the central bank's forecasting ability and information supply: too much noise makes markets rely on official guidance, creating moral hazard and bubbles. Peter Fisher similarly argues that central bank 'certainty' makes markets less risk-sensitive. The two may push for reducing rather than increasing information releases. Warsh's 'hall of mirrors' metaphor in his speech already admits markets aren't always right.

34:51 Economists entering AI companies lose their independent voice
Posen argues that the rush of economists to AI companies is not unprecedented—it happened during the internet era—but this time it's more troubling. Companies like Anthropic hire economists partly to design AI transition policies, and these scholars genuinely believe they're doing good. The problem is that once inside, they enter the corporate hierarchy, losing independent voice and freedom to choose topics, and their views are reasonably discounted by outsiders. Posen's hope is that scholars stay in research institutes, earning low six-figure salaries, while retaining public influence.

38:53 AI displacement hasn't happened yet; programmer employment is still growing
Posen says labor market data doesn't yet show AI displacement—even programmer and truck driver employment growth continues. Brynjolfsson's J-curve theory holds that firms need time to reorganize, and there will be a period of human-AI collaboration first. Garicano's messy jobs theory points out that seemingly automatable jobs actually contain a lot of tacit knowledge and interpersonal relations—truck drivers don't just drive. Large-scale displacement may take about five years, and it will first show up in reduced hiring of young people.

54:13 Rates will be 75-100 basis points higher six months from now
Posen reiterates his earlier forecast of 4% year-end PCE inflation, which is materializing; CPI has already exceeded 4% early in the year. The bigger issue is inflation inertia: while energy prices may cause a slight dip in the next month or two, core services inflation is sticky, with 3/6/12-month moving averages all rising. He expects the Fed to hike in September or December; if September, December will follow. Six months from now, the federal funds rate will be 75-100 basis points higher than today, and only then will inflation begin to truly decline, hovering in the 3.5%-4.5% range in the meantime.

item.title: ECT Is Not Torture: 70% Improve, 60% Recover
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-tpwky-ect-不是酷刑-是精神科最有效的疗法之一/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-tpwky-ect-不是酷刑-是精神科最有效的疗法之一/
item.description: ECT helps about 70% of patients improve and 60% see symptoms disappear; it is not the electric torture of One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, but the oldest somatic therapy to survive from the slaughterhouse to the anti-psychiatry movement and beyond.
item.content:encoded:
ECT helps about 70% of patients improve and 60% see symptoms disappear; it is not the electric torture of One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, but the oldest somatic therapy to survive from the slaughterhouse to the anti-psychiatry movement and beyond.

Historical narratives often swing between two extremes: either barbaric torture or miracle cure. This episode puts efficacy, abuse, media amplification, and patient accounts together, showing where the stigma comes from and why it is not the whole picture today.

1:03 The heaviest side effect is not memory loss but stigma
The episode opens with nurse Elan's firsthand account: she had been depressed since childhood, and after medications failed, she chose ECT. She says that after three treatments, colors seemed more saturated and the world became approachable again. Side effects are real: for days after treatment she could not name nouns, got lost in familiar neighborhoods, and lost words mid-conversation; long-term memories from before treatment remain, but it feels like the room has been rearranged. She states clearly that the heaviest side effect is the stigma surrounding ECT—she worries that sharing her experience will change how others see her, and she believes that stigma is why doctors did not recommend ECT earlier.

7:53 Fear of ECT is not innate; film taught it
A 2016 global survey of film and television found that 81% of movies and 72% of TV shows portray ECT inaccurately and negatively. In the most famous example, One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, Jack Nicholson is strapped down and conscious during the shock, a scene close to torture. A few positive portrayals exist, such as in Homeland and Call the Midwife, but they are rare. The hosts' judgment: public fear of ECT does not arise from nowhere; it is a media stigma reinforced by decades of film and TV, which can make people unwilling even to consider ECT.

13:07 ECT is the most effective psychiatric intervention available
ECT treats severe mental illness like treatment-resistant depression by applying electrical current to the brain to induce a seizure; today it is done under anesthesia and muscle relaxation, with strict informed consent. Two figures are often overlooked: about 70% of people improve and about 60% achieve clinical remission, making it one of the most effective psychiatric interventions available. Compared with patient responses to SSRIs discussed in earlier episodes, it is especially effective for treatment-resistant cases that do not respond to antidepressants alone.

17:09 Electricity is just a tool; the target was always seizure
Shock therapies that emerged in the 1920s were not originally electrical: insulin coma therapy put patients into hypoglycemic coma and convulsions, and Metrosol chemical shock therapy used drugs to induce seizures. Doctors pursued this path because they observed that epilepsy and schizophrenia rarely coexisted, and some catatonic patients improved after spontaneous seizures, so they treated the seizure itself as the key therapeutic ingredient. Cerletti later turned to electricity to find a safer, more tolerable way to induce seizures. Electricity is just a tool; the target is seizure.

22:14 ECT's technical origin is pigs in a slaughterhouse
Cerletti's starting point was the slaughterhouse: workers stunned pigs with electric shocks, and some pigs had seizures afterward. In April 1938, a man in Rome who was incoherent and brought in by police became the first human subject. Without anesthesia or muscle relaxants, the first two shocks did not induce a seizure. On the third, with a higher dose, he had a grand mal seizure, briefly stopped breathing and turned cyanotic, then after forty-five seconds took a deep breath and recovered. Cerletti later reported 36 cases: 11 complete remissions, 20 improvements, and 5 no change.

31:26 It spread so fast because informed consent did not exist
By 1941, just three years after the first human trial, 42% of psychiatric hospitals in the U.S. had ECT machines. Several reasons explain the rapid spread: it was seen as an improved version of existing shock therapies with a low barrier to entry; doctors were desperate for chronic, severely ill patients; ECT was not the only treatment but often part of a recovery path alongside psychotherapy; early patient reports were generally positive; and there was no informed consent or extended trial period to protect patients. That last point planted the seeds for widespread distrust of psychiatry.

36:34 Using ECT as punishment is not a movie invention
The negative history is not fictional: some institutions used ECT to treat homosexuality or hysteria; 1940s records admit that shock-induced amnesia and disorientation could quiet patients and keep them from disrupting ward order. Such abuses occurred mostly in institutions with fewer resources and more marginalized patients—not in all hospitals—but when exposed, they sparked public outrage. The anti-psychiatry movement then framed mental illness itself as social control. The hosts do not excuse these actions; they only remind us that with few effective drugs and severely overcrowded wards, both doctors and families were trapped in desperation.

42:45 The anti-psychiatry movement forced ECT to prove itself
The anti-psychiatry movement drastically reduced ECT use in the 1960s and 1970s, but it also forced ECT to undergo stricter scrutiny and randomized controlled trials. The result: it is the only major somatic therapy that has survived from before the era of psychopharmacology and passed the tests. After the 1980s, public accounts by Dick Cavett, Carrie Fisher, and psychologist Norman Endler brought positive narratives back. Memory loss remains a real controversy: research says long-term effects are rare, but some patients feel their experience is not fully captured by measurement tools. The experience cannot be reduced to one star or five stars; it should be neither glorified nor stigmatized.

item.title: China's Economic Peak Has Passed: Credit Dries Up, Deflation Ahead
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-geopoliticsdec-中国经济巅峰已过-美国优势还将扩大/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-geopoliticsdec-中国经济巅峰已过-美国优势还将扩大/
item.description: China's share of global GDP peaked in 2021 and has been declining since; credit growth has fallen from 18% to 5%, and real growth may be only 1.5%-2%; the US has outperformed for five consecutive years. The narrative of industrial chain dominance is disproven by data; the future looks more like Japan-style deflation.
item.content:encoded:
China's share of global GDP peaked in 2021 and has been declining since; credit growth has fallen from 18% to 5%, and real growth may be only 1.5%-2%; the US has outperformed for five consecutive years. The narrative of industrial chain dominance is disproven by data; the future looks more like Japan-style deflation.

To counter the mainstream narrative that 'China's new industries = growth engine,' grounding judgments in verifiable data on credit, special bonds, and demographics; for those who want to update their long-term view of China and the US.

0:05 China has already missed its window to overtake the US
Dmitri sets the tone with official data: China's share of global GDP peaked at 18.5% in 2021 and has declined each year since; the US has risen from 24% to about 26%. He concludes that China has almost no chance of replacing the US as the world's largest economy, and the US economic advantage may continue to widen over the next decade. Logan fully agrees and steers the discussion toward a 'decline, not collapse' framework.

2:11 The root of China's slowdown is the end of credit expansion
Logan attributes China's slowdown to the end of extraordinary credit expansion. After the financial crisis, China added credit equivalent to one-third of global GDP in eight years; credit growth fell from an average of 18% in 2007-2016 to 9% after 2017, and now stands at just over 5%. Once credit stops, borrowers can no longer refinance, and investment slows. Official figures still report 5.2% growth in 2023 and 5% for 2024 and 2025, but he estimates real growth since 2022 has been only 1.5%-2%, already below the US.

6:14 Using purchasing power parity rewards deflation
Addressing the common rebuttal that 'China has already surpassed the US in PPP terms,' Logan says PPP comparisons are still meaningful for developing countries but untenable between the world's two largest economies: scoring by PPP rewards China for producing deflation—the lower domestic prices are, the stronger the economy appears, yet deflation is precisely the problem. He also stresses that debt is repaid in nominal local currency, so nominal GDP matters; the exchange rate is not an exogenous variable but an external signal of China's policy capacity.

13:25 Capital controls are not a cure, only buy time
Logan acknowledges that China's capital controls are effective but argues they are not a panacea for massive macro imbalances. The impossible trinity dictates that free capital flow, exchange rate stability, and monetary policy independence can only be achieved two at a time. The function of capital controls is to delay outflows, suppress rapid cross-border volatility, and channel outflows into government-visible channels—Huawei and BYD can go global aggressively, while private firms like HNA had their overseas acquisitions halted in 2016; this is the two sides of the same screening mechanism.

17:35 Credit still subsidizes old industries, not shifting to new ones
Logan rebuts the claim that 'credit is shifting to more productive new industries': central bank data show that the share of loans issued at or below the Loan Prime Rate has risen from the 20s percent to 59%, indicating banks are continuously subsidizing. The share of special revenue bonds directed to so-called strategic industries rose only from about 2% in 2021 to 6% in 2025, with the vast majority still flowing to traditional sectors. Using the 2023 input-output table, he estimates that electric vehicles, batteries, AI, solar, etc., together account for about 6.3% of GDP, while the decline in real estate and infrastructure investment is about six times the increase in these new industries.

27:45 Europe is the last buyer of China's excess capacity
Logan judges that if Europe turns protectionist, China will be 'truly finished': the US market has narrowed and transshipment space is limited, and the developing world cannot absorb China's excess capacity while maintaining its own growth. He warns that the US is wrong to focus only on bilateral deficits—deficits are determined by the savings-investment gap; tariffs only redistribute deficits, and not addressing the underlying imbalance will only breed more transshipment trade.

34:58 Without touching taxes, domestic demand won't take off
Logan draws a parallel with Soviet Premier Kosygin's reforms: Brezhnev chose to pivot to a technological revolution rather than push reforms and maintain ideology. To convert savings into consumption, China's real lever is tax policy—extracting resources from high-net-worth individuals, state-owned enterprises, and private firms excluded from the financial system. But he thinks it is almost unimaginable that Xi Jinping would go on TV to announce that 'the fiscal and financial system of the past 15 years will no longer apply in the future'; Beijing's insistence on the 5% growth narrative is partly to undermine export controls and discourage Western investment in alternative supply chains.

39:00 China in 2035 will look like Japan today
Logan predicts that without major policy changes, China's economy in 2035 will resemble Japan's: persistent deflation, persistent external surpluses, exchange rate depreciation pressure, and low interest rates. The hardest constraint is demographics—China's actual average age at death is 73, and the early PRC baby boom will bring a population decline of 50-60 million over the next decade, about 3%-4% of the total population; even maintaining last year's low birth rate of 7.92 million won't stop it. He also reminds that the fiscal deficit is already close to $2 trillion per year, about 9.5% of GDP, leaving far fewer resources available than in the past. Finally, he says that if China truly wins through export share, it will invite stronger political backlash—'winning is losing.'

item.title: Bell Used Einstein's Own Tools to Refute His Central Argument
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-theoriesofever-贝尔用爱因斯坦自己的工具推翻了他的核心论点/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-theoriesofever-贝尔用爱因斯坦自己的工具推翻了他的核心论点/
item.category: Theories of Everything with Curt Jaimungal
item.description: The EPR argument forces you to choose between an incomplete quantum description and action at a distance; determinism was never an assumption but a conclusion inferred from the argument. The full logic of Bell's theorem must start here.
item.content:encoded:
The EPR argument forces you to choose between an incomplete quantum description and action at a distance; determinism was never an assumption but a conclusion inferred from the argument. The full logic of Bell's theorem must start here.

Maudlin traces the story from Einstein's 1905 photoelectric effect paper to Bell's 1964 inequality, breaking the EPR argument into steps that can be checked one by one. For those who want to truly understand nonlocality rather than memorize conclusions.

3:05 The father of quantum theory is not Planck but Einstein
Although Planck is usually regarded as the father of quantum theory, it was Einstein's 1905 photoelectric effect paper that actually proposed the quantization hypothesis. Planck only did statistical calculations, while Einstein explicitly argued that energy is transferred in discrete quanta. Maudlin deliberately corrects this historical attribution.

45:32 A single particle is enough to force action at a distance
Einstein's objection at the 1927 Solvay Conference was: if the wave function completely describes a single particle, and the wave spreads in all directions toward the screen, then the particle could act at multiple locations simultaneously. To avoid multiple points of action, one must introduce an instantaneous and global collapse mechanism of the wave function—this is action at a distance. Note, this is not about superluminal signaling.

1:14:50 If the wave function is real, locality has no place to reside
The wave function of a many-particle system is defined on configuration space, not physical space; for example, a two-particle system is six-dimensional configuration space. In classical mechanics, configuration space is a mathematical convenience, but if the wave function is taken as fundamental reality, configuration space becomes the physical stage, and the definition of local forces in each small spatial region becomes problematic. This is another layer of Einstein's concern about dynamical locality.

1:31:59 EPR's reality criterion cannot be coherently denied
EPR's reality criterion says: if, without disturbing a system, one can predict with probability 1 the value of a physical quantity, then that quantity corresponds to an element of physical reality. Maudlin emphasizes that this is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one. He refutes common attempts to deny the criterion, arguing that it is analytic and cannot be coherently denied. This sets the stage for the subsequent either-or conclusion.

2:02:26 Either the description is incomplete or accept action at a distance
Since the reality criterion cannot be denied, the EPR argument forces a choice: either accept that the quantum description is incomplete, or accept that Alice's operation in her lab indeed disturbs the physical state of Bob's particle—that is, action at a distance. Einstein found action at a distance absurd and therefore chose incompleteness. This is the logical exit of the entire EPR argument.

2:10:34 Denying determinism does not escape Bell's conclusion
Maudlin repeatedly emphasizes that in the EPR argument determinism is not assumed but inferred from perfect correlations and locality. He quotes Bell's own words: 'Insofar as determinism plays a role in the EPR argument, it is not assumed but inferred.' Therefore, attempts to escape Bell's conclusion by denying determinism are completely ineffective.

2:43:53 Bohr's famous response was understood by no one
Faced with the EPR argument, Bohr had only two logically possible responses: accept action at a distance, or admit the incompleteness of quantum description. But Bohr chose neither. Maudlin says his response paper is 'a mess' that no one can understand. He even mentions that in the book edited by Wheeler and Zurek, two pages of Bohr's article are reversed in order, yet no one noticed because no one could follow the logic anyway.

2:55:02 Any local theory gives wrong predictions
Bell's starting point was precisely the EPR paper, yet his conclusion was that Einstein's fundamental claim about 'no action at a distance' was wrong: any local theory fails to make correct predictions. Maudlin calls this a great ironic reversal—Bell used Einstein's own tools to refute his fundamental argument. This is the true entry point for understanding why Bell's theorem matters.

item.title: Quantum's Endgame Is Not Cleaner Qubits, It's Who Can Mass-Produce with Phone-Chip Fabs
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-fromfirstprinc-硅自旋将赢-百万比特只需一块硅晶圆/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-fromfirstprinc-硅自旋将赢-百万比特只需一块硅晶圆/
item.description: Quantum computing's endgame is not who has cleaner qubits, but who can mass-produce using existing semiconductor fabs; silicon spin qubits reuse TSMC lithography, while ion traps are stuck at 100,000 laser beams and superconductors at warehouse-sized refrigerators.
item.content:encoded:
Quantum computing's endgame is not who has cleaner qubits, but who can mass-produce using existing semiconductor fabs; silicon spin qubits reuse TSMC lithography, while ion traps are stuck at 100,000 laser beams and superconductors at warehouse-sized refrigerators.

The exclusive value is in the second half: HRL paper's CNOT error rate, AI auto-tuning, and FFP's striking scores; the first half's physics primer is more educational, veterans can fast-forward.

0:00 Ion traps and superconductors need miracles first; silicon doesn't
To build a 100,000-qubit ion trap, you'd first need to invent the optical miracle of 100,000 laser beams; for a million superconducting qubits, you'd need a warehouse-sized cryostat; a million spin qubits only require standard 300mm silicon wafers, run through the same lithography equipment that TSMC, ASML, and Intel use to make phone processors. Krishna uses this to set the tone for the whole episode: the key to the quantum race is not single-qubit fidelity, but whether the scaling path already exists in the industrial system.

32:48 Quantum computing is no longer about principles, it's about engineering
In 2000, DiVincenzo proposed five criteria, aiming to dismiss liquid-state NMR quantum computing. This episode, FFP proposes its own three criteria: qubit quality, control, scalability and economics. The rest of the episode scores four routes—superconducting, ion trap, neutral atom, silicon spin—item by item. Laying out the evaluation system itself tells you: quantum computing has entered the stage of engineering competition; you can't just talk about principles.

1:24:33 Superconductors aren't a technical failure, they're an engineering impossibility
Estimates show that 1,000 logical qubits require 10 million transmon physical qubits. Control line count is limited by the cooling capacity of dilution refrigerators, frequency crowding occurs, and helium-3 supply becomes a new resource constraint. FFP gives superconductors only 1/10 on scalability and economics, with a total score of 11/30. This is the first time the show separates "technically strong" from "engineering infeasible"; a warehouse-sized refrigerator means even data centers might not fit it.

1:47:08 Ion traps win on coherence time, lose on gate speed
Ion trap coherence times reach ten hours, but gate operations rely on phonons and are limited by Paul trap oscillation frequencies, making them about 1,000 times slower than superconducting. The result is counterintuitive: even if ion traps could scale to break encryption, cracking 2048-bit RSA would take about a year, while superconducting would take only about eight hours. Long coherence time doesn't mean more work per unit time; for practical computation, slow gate time is a throughput disaster.

2:03:32 The quantum threat is neither tomorrow nor never
A March 2026 paper from Harvard, Caltech, and Qera says 10,000 qubits might break internet encryption, but it would actually take years; even with 100,000 physical qubits, under mathematically optimal assumptions, breaking RSA would take about three months. This number strikes both extreme narratives: the quantum threat is not tomorrow, but it is also never far away. To achieve "breakable within months," qubit count, gate speed, and error correction must all be met simultaneously.

2:50:02 Quantum companies' fate is in government contracts
HRL lost key project funding in early 2026 and laid off 376 people. Government funding shifted from basic research to applied research demanding rapid commercialization; IBM and Intel received support from the CHIPS Act, and ultimately IBM acquired HRL. Krishna calls this the debut of quantum computing's MVP: quantum companies live or die by government contracts, and being acquired is not failure but a way for the technology to enter an industrial system with manufacturing capability.

3:23:10 A million qubits can't be tuned by hand; it's image recognition
Automated tuning becomes key to scaling: a 2023 paper could tune six electrons by hand, but manual tuning of a million qubits would take a human lifetime. Tuning is essentially image recognition—when scanning voltage, tunneling events appear as stripes; Krishna's team uses DETR combined with ResNet and Transformer to automatically recognize stripes and generate parameters. This is also the hidden premise for why silicon spin can reuse semiconductor fabs: no matter how many qubits, software can auto-align them.

3:32:31 Silicon may not be first, but it will be the last to win
FFP's final scores: silicon spin gets 10/10 on qubit quality, 10/10 on control (assuming isotope enrichment and valley state issues are solved), and 10000/10 on scalability and economics, for a total of 10020/30; neutral atoms score negative 3000. Krishna admits silicon may not be the first route to achieve fault tolerance, but once it does, it will become the final standard, like transistors replacing vacuum tubes, because it's cheap and manufacturable.

item.title: AI Chip Shipments Will Jump an Order of Magnitude: From a Million to 15 Million
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-techtechpotato-未来-ai-定制芯片的形态-一只带-16-个-hbm-的巨兽/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-techtechpotato-未来-ai-定制芯片的形态-一只带-16-个-hbm-的巨兽/
item.description: Broadcom's president reveals an AI chip roadmap: from a million units to 15 million, with the 'beast' being the largest package of 8 stackable compute dies plus 16 HBM modules, and four of the five frontier labs are collaborating.
item.content:encoded:
Broadcom's president reveals an AI chip roadmap: from a million units to 15 million, with the 'beast' being the largest package of 8 stackable compute dies plus 16 HBM modules, and four of the five frontier labs are collaborating.

Broadcom rarely discloses details, but this time it gave three tiers of packaging and three tiers of shipment volumes, plus a clear judgment on the HBM bottleneck. For those tracking ASICs and packaging, these 11 minutes are more informative than many long analyses.

1:06 Custom chip makers still outsource the final step
Google, Meta, Amazon, and some frontier model companies can have their own chip design teams, define their own architecture and interconnect, but ultimately they still have to 'get the thing built': dealing with foundries and development kits, managing the timing and latency of connections between transistors. Broadcom is the largest of these fee-based back-end design service providers. Clients come to it not just for design capability but also for a batch of ready-made IP including high-speed I/O, high-performance compute, and memory controllers.

3:09 The most tight-lipped chip company suddenly starts talking
Broadcom is an enigma externally: it has almost no PR department and rarely discloses proactively. Occasionally it releases a Tomahawk networking chip or chats with Patrick Kennedy on ServeTheHome. Over the past year, President Charlie has unusually taken the stage at launch events to talk about what Broadcom is doing and why it has expanded its customer base from traditional networking chips to custom AI chips. The chart showing three tiers of chips is the clue.

4:09 Today's AI servers are only the smallest of three tiers
Of the three tiers Charlie showed, the leftmost is already shipping in hundreds of thousands of systems, about the size of this Cisco chip on the desk: a central compute die surrounded by four to six HBM modules, packaged using something like TSMC's CoWoS. Broadcom says that over the past year, more than a million of these chips have shipped to customers. This tier is the reality of today's AI servers.

5:09 Larger packages actually ship in higher volumes
The middle tier is noticeably larger: two to four compute/I/O dies surrounded by eight to twelve HBM modules; AMD's MI455X also fits this design form. Charlie's expected shipment volumes are key: the middle tier is expected to ship 5 million units, and the rightmost tier 15 million. Placed next to 'one million in the past year,' this is not linear growth but an order-of-magnitude jump in shipments for the next generation of custom AI chips.

6:11 The rightmost chip may stack compute dies on compute dies
The rightmost 'beast': the red parts are eight compute dies arranged in two columns of four rows, and they are stacked. Charlie lifted the red to reveal purple underneath, which could be SRAM, or SRAM might be on top; if it is compute-on-compute, it effectively equals sixteen compute dies. Each compute die is paired with two HBM modules, so one package contains sixteen HBM modules, with two light-blue I/O dies at the top and bottom edges, and openings left at the package edges for optical modules.

7:11 Almost all frontier model companies are making their own chips
Charlie said that four of the five most advanced frontier model labs are working with Broadcom on custom compute chips. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic define the designs they want, Broadcom does the back-end services and interfaces with TSMC, and then partners like Supermicro and WiWynn are brought in for data-center-scale deployment. This also explains why Broadcom is expanding capacity: it not only serves traditional networking customers but is also taking orders from large model companies.

9:11 The bottleneck to scaling may not be packaging but HBM
What may truly be the bottleneck is not packaging but whether there is enough high-bandwidth memory to go around: will new forms between DDR/LPDDR and HBM emerge to fill the gap? Additionally, Broadcom said on stage that it has already deployed a 2nm chip with a partner, slightly smaller than the beast, and closer in time. This reminds us that in the coming years, advanced packaging and HBM capacity will be swept up along with custom chip orders.

10:13 The first 2nm custom chip to land may come from Japan
The host pinned down the 'soon-to-ship, smaller' 2nm chip Broadcom mentioned: he asked George from Chips and Cheese, and the two judged it to be Fujitsu's Monaka—a 2nm compute die paired with a 5nm SRAM die, with a central I/O die in the middle. This chip has previously appeared as a mockup or test silicon at several conferences.

item.title: An Explorer Died for a Fictional City, Born from a Political Forgery
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-stuffmissed-福西特不是去冒险-是去给橡胶资本画地图/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-stuffmissed-福西特不是去冒险-是去给橡胶资本画地图/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Percy Fawcett's Amazon expeditions are often told as adventure legends, but the real starting point was border disputes fueled by the rubber trade; his narrative of 'respect' for indigenous people is a gross oversimplification, and the City of Z that obsessed him may rest on a forged manuscript.
item.content:encoded:
Percy Fawcett's Amazon expeditions are often told as adventure legends, but the real starting point was border disputes fueled by the rubber trade; his narrative of 'respect' for indigenous people is a gross oversimplification, and the City of Z that obsessed him may rest on a forged manuscript.

This episode has medium information density, but it clearly lays out the beginnings of the rubber trade, indigenous catastrophe, and Manuscript 512; listeners only after adventure yarns may find the first half's setup a bit long.

3:04 His obsession began with a childhood Roman well
Fawcett was born in 1867. His family was nominally aristocratic, but his father, Edward Fawcett, had squandered the fortune and could only serve as a private secretary to Queen Victoria's son 'Bertie' (later Edward VII). Fawcett described a loveless childhood in Torquay that made him introverted. His sister recalled that as a child he discovered a well full of Roman pottery on Halden Moors and had his siblings lower him down to retrieve the artifacts and take them to a museum. This boldness, stubbornness, and outward-seeking personality later resurfaced in his fixation on the occult and the Amazon.

8:13 An officer who held séances still rose to major
In 1901 Fawcett married Nina, and in 1903 their first son Jack was born; that same year he was posted to Spike Island off the south coast of Ireland. Fawcett found the posting dull, so he spent his spare time conducting séances. His interest in the occult was not a fringe hobby; his son Brian later wrote that anyone who sought knowledge beyond the material might be called a mystic. This interest did not hinder his military career—he was promoted to major. It shows that Fawcett's 'rationality' and 'superstition' coexisted, foreshadowing his later credulity toward Manuscript 512.

10:19 His first Amazon trip was a diplomatic assignment, not adventure
In 1901 Fawcett joined the Royal Geographical Society and completed specialized training in boundary demarcation. In 1906 the Society's president, Sir George Goldie, met with him, asked about his knowledge of Bolivia, and then explained: border disputes among Brazil, Peru, and Bolivia had escalated because of the rubber trade. The countries involved would not accept demarcation by any interested party, so the Bolivian government asked the Royal Geographical Society to arbitrate and recommend an officer. For Fawcett, this was a chance to 'escape the monotony of an artillery officer's life'; he was 39, and his wife was pregnant with their second child. The chain of argument here is: rubber's economic value → territorial disputes → Britain as a 'disinterested' third party → Fawcett enters the Amazon as a surveyor. The counterintuitive point is that his initial expedition was not self-directed adventure but commercial and diplomatic arrangement.

14:25 He was attacked everywhere because 90% of natives were already dead
Before he reached South America, the rubber industry had already transformed the region. Figures cited in the episode: before Europeans arrived, the area of present-day Brazil had at least 2,000 indigenous tribes with a total population of about 11 million; in the first hundred years after colonists arrived in the 16th century, 90% of indigenous people died from disease or genocide, and survivors were often enslaved for rubber work. The rubber trade made land extremely valuable, and Europeans moved in and seized indigenous lands, leading natives to view all Europeans as threats—this is the backdrop to Fawcett's hostile encounters. His own writings also show he was well aware of European colonial atrocities. This section provides a structural explanation for 'why he was attacked everywhere' and corrects the romanticized narrative of 'explorer in peril.'

17:28 Calling him respectful of natives sets the bar too low
Fawcett's dealings with indigenous people were not solely confrontational. He would insist that he and his companions lay down their arms and show they posed no threat; he learned local languages and condemned the earlier European colonists for creating the problems that continued to sour relations. But at the same time, much of what he wrote was 'extremely racist' and condescending. The hosts state plainly that the common later claim that he 'respected indigenous people' is an oversimplification; even if he was 'often better' than contemporary European explorers, that bar was appallingly low. The value here: many popular narratives today cast Fawcett as an enlightened explorer, and the episode dismantles that myth with specific written evidence, without reducing his behavior to pure villainy.

19:28 He survived an ambush with an accordion, not a gun
This is one of Fawcett's most famous escape stories. His expedition was ambushed on a river by indigenous archers, and peaceful calls went unanswered. He had his companion Todd sit on a log mid-river with an accordion and start playing, while the others sang loudly and stomped their feet. Before long, the hail of arrows stopped, and a wide-eyed native peered out from the bushes; the expedition was then welcomed into the village and even given help. This example shows Fawcett was not only about force; his tools for problem-solving included music and clownish performance. It also shows his records contain both observations worth taking seriously and plenty of unreliable exaggeration, setting up contrasts with later descriptions of giant anacondas, peanuts, and double-nosed dogs.

25:32 He believed in a lost city because old documents really mentioned one
Before World War I, Fawcett efficiently completed his mapping (often much faster than expected) while becoming increasingly fascinated by claims of lost cities in the jungle. He named the city he sought 'Zed' and located it in the non-coastal southern Brazilian state of Mato Grosso; that area covers about 900,000 square kilometers, is densely forested, and remains one of Brazil's least densely populated regions even today, with almost no European entry in the early 20th century. The chain of argument: numerous 16th- and 17th-century Spanish and Portuguese explorer documents described 'very advanced large cities' → Fawcett believed they were real → he grew increasingly obsessed with finding the City of Z.

29:40 The manuscript he believed without reservation may be a hoax
After the war, Fawcett continued studying old documents, most famously Manuscript 512, held in the National Library of Rio de Janeiro: a Portuguese adventurer's 1753 account of his travels in the Amazon, sometimes attributed to João de Silvestre de Moraes. Fawcett gave the author the pseudonym Francisco Raposo and wrote that he believed the manuscript's contents 'without reservation,' calling it an 'incomparable story.' However, at the start of the episode the hosts had already warned that this document 'is likely a hoax.' So the real suspense is not whether the lost city existed, but why a trained geography officer would be so captivated by a possibly forged 1753 record.

item.title: Time Is Not an Illusion: Irreversibility Is More Fundamental Than Symmetric Equations
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-mindscape-时间的方向性比时间对称方程更根本/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-mindscape-时间的方向性比时间对称方程更根本/
item.description: Jim Al-Khalili argues that time is real and directed, and that irreversibility is more fundamental than time-symmetric equations; he also proposes using quantum entanglement entropy instead of thermodynamic entropy as the basis for the past hypothesis.
item.content:encoded:
Jim Al-Khalili argues that time is real and directed, and that irreversibility is more fundamental than time-symmetric equations; he also proposes using quantum entanglement entropy instead of thermodynamic entropy as the basis for the past hypothesis.

Sean Carroll and Jim Al-Khalili hold opposing views on the arrow of time, and this episode reveals their real points of disagreement; the second half also covers mechanisms in quantum biology and a new hypothesis about quantum entanglement entropy.

4:07 The direction of time is built in, not emergent
Jim takes a hard stance: time is real and tangible, part of four-dimensional spacetime, not just something clocks measure. He goes further, saying that the directionality of time is not emergent from directionless fundamental laws but is built into the universe. Sean reminds the audience that this is highly controversial—many physicists think time is just a tool or that direction is a product of coarse-graining. Jim's intuition is that, seen from inside the universe, irreversibility is the more fundamental thing.

17:38 No system is isolated, so irreversibility is the norm
The traditional narrative is that fundamental equations like Newton's and Schrödinger's are invariant under time reversal, and the arrow of time must emerge from entropy increase or coarse-graining. Jim turns this around: time-symmetric equations are idealizations because no system is truly isolated—even quantum systems are constantly entangled with their environment. Time-symmetric equations apply only to isolated systems and are a special case of the master equation; in reality, everything exchanges energy and information with its environment, and irreversibility is the norm. He admits this is a minority view but thinks it is closer to the real world.

27:50 The special moment must be at the Big Bang, not last week
If the whole universe is treated as an isolated system that also obeys time-symmetric laws, then by the second law, yesterday's entropy should be higher than today's, not lower. The only way out is to push that special moment to the very beginning: the Big Bang. That is the past hypothesis. Jim stresses that this is not an extra assumption but part of the universe's initial conditions, alongside fine-tuning of constants. He agrees with Sean: if you must pick a special moment, the Big Bang is far more reasonable than last week.

31:03 The laws of physics contain no flow of time, yet we feel it
Even if low-entropy initial conditions explain the arrow of time, Sean presses: where do psychological experiences like 'now' and the sense of passage come from? Jim honestly admits that the laws of physics contain no flow of time, yet we feel time flowing. He says this is a gap between physical time and manifest time, and he is not even sure how to articulate it clearly. This candor is more valuable than pretending to have solved it, and it shows the problem of time is far from closed.

45:51 DNA mutations may come from a proton's quantum tunneling
From a nuclear physicist's perspective, Jim presents the most concrete case in quantum biology: the two strands of DNA are held together by hydrogen bonds, and the hydrogen atom is essentially a proton. Löwdin proposed in the early 1960s that a proton could quantum-tunnel through the energy barrier to the opposite strand, causing mutations during replication. Jim's team has done increasingly refined calculations to determine the ratio of tunneling to thermal excitation. He points out that quantum biology is not the old saw that 'atoms are quantum' but asks whether life has evolved to exploit long-lived coherence and entanglement.

1:03:12 A more fundamental version of the past hypothesis uses entanglement entropy
The thermodynamic past hypothesis requires specifying a low-entropy microstate. Jim and philosopher Eddy Chen have tried a more quantum version: assume the universe began in a pure state with extremely low entanglement entropy, with subsystems barely entangled. As it evolves, subsystems become increasingly entangled, and the entanglement entropy of the whole universe rises monotonically. Conceptually this is more fundamental than thermodynamic entropy, but Jim admits there are many gaps—for instance, how finely to partition subsystems. This direction is still unfinished.

1:12:29 After the heat death of the universe, time still passes
Many say time might disappear at extreme scales. Jim counters: even tens of trillions of years from now, when the universe reaches thermal equilibrium and no change can be used to measure time, time still passes. He admits this is not time in the relativistic sense that holds in every reference frame, but it makes time almost like Newton's absolute clock—a real happening. For him, even if time emerges from something more fundamental, that does not mean it is not real.

item.title: Most Gazans Have Abandoned Hamas, and the Window for Disarmament Is Opening
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-econtalk-加沙多数人已抛弃哈马斯-缴械窗口正在打开/
